ColumnSchemaOut.description:
One result column's name and DuckDB logical type.

``type`` is spelled the way DuckDB itself prints a logical type — the same
string ``DESCRIBE`` returns in its ``column_type`` column. That spelling is
self-describing and re-parses exactly, including parameterized and nested
types (``DECIMAL(38,10)``, ``STRUCT(a INTEGER, b VARCHAR)``, ``ENUM('e', 'f')``,
``INTEGER[2]``), so no separate precision/scale fields are carried.

No ``nullable`` field: DuckDB relations carry no reliable nullability
(``DESCRIBE`` reports ``YES`` unconditionally), so reporting it would be
inventing data.

delete.description:
Ask the agent to stop a running query.

Best effort and idempotent: cancelling a query that already finished is a
no-op, not an error. The query row survives -- cancellation is a terminal
status, not a deletion.

get.description:
One query's status, timings and error, by its global id.

Addressed globally rather than under its workspace: the id is unique, and the
submitter already holds it. Any member of the query's workspace may read it,
which is what makes the history an audit trail.

Pass `wait_timeout_s` to hold the response until the query reaches a terminal
state, for a client following a statement that outlived the wait on submit.
It is **opt-in and defaults to 0** deliberately: this is also the route the
worksheet refreshes several times a second and the history reads, and neither
wants a held request. Capped by `SQL_STATEMENT_MAX_WAIT_TIMEOUT_S`.

get.description:
A finished query's whole result in a columnar format.

Exact where JSON is not: every value keeps its type (DECIMAL as decimal,
64-bit and wider integers as integers), and the result streams in one response
instead of 1000-row pages. `column_schema` on the query names each column's
DuckDB type. Guarded exactly like `/rows`.

post.description:
Run a statement on this session's DuckDB connection. 200 if it finished
within `wait_timeout_s`, 202 with a query id if it is still running.

Unlike `POST /workspaces/{workspace}/queries`, this reuses one held connection, so
temp tables, `SET`s and attached catalogs persist between statements. 409 if
the session is not open.

The call blocks for up to `wait_timeout_s` (server default
`SQL_STATEMENT_WAIT_TIMEOUT_S`, `0` to never block) so a client learns the
statement finished when it does, instead of on its own next poll. A statement
that outlives the budget comes back 202 and is polled through
`GET /queries/{id}` as before — it is never cancelled for outrunning a wait.

get.description:
Every catalog, schema and table the caller may see in the workspace, with
each table's columns in DuckDB types when `columns=true`.

Filtered by grant: an object the caller holds no tier on is left out, as in
the catalog tree. Names need no compute. Columns are described by an agent;
with none connected and elastic compute on, compute is started and the call
waits, answering 503 `compute_starting` if it is not up in time. At most
`METADATA_COLUMNS_MAX_TABLES` tables are described per request.

post.description:
Submit SQL for execution. Accepted, not completed: 202 with a query id.

Dispatch picks a connected agent the caller may use, so 503 means no
compatible compute is available rather than that the SQL was wrong. Poll
`GET /queries/{query_id}` for status and read results from
`GET /queries/{query_id}/rows`.

A read whose tables are unchanged since an identical query ran is answered
from the result cache instead: the 202 then carries a query that is already
`done`, with `cache_status` "hit". Send `use_cache: false` to always run.

Send `wait_timeout_s` to block until the run finishes, up to that many seconds:
the answer is then 200 with the finished query, or 202 if it is still going.

post.description:
A query's result columns and their DuckDB types, without running it.

The statement is bound by an agent (`DESCRIBE`), never executed, so it reads
no rows, and the caller needs only the `metadata` tier on the tables it names.
With no agent connected and elastic compute on, compute is started and the
call waits for it, answering 503 `compute_starting` if it is not up in time.
Statements that return no grid (DML, DDL) answer with `columns: null` without
touching an agent.

post.description:
Open a session, starting compute first when none is up.

Synchronous by contract — it returns a session a client can immediately run
statements on — so when compute has to start it holds the request rather than
parking silently. `wait_timeout_s`/`on_wait_timeout` choose how long and what
happens at the end: 503 + Retry-After (the default, for a client that cannot
poll) or 202 with a pending session (for one that can).

202.description: Compute is still starting and `on_wait_timeout=continue` was set. Poll `GET /sql/sessions/{session_id}` until it reports `open`.
